html:
The cedar of Lebanon is a great evergreen tree of the mountains of Lebanon whose fragrant, lasting wood was prized across the ancient Near East. Egypt was importing it by about 2600 BCE.

An Egyptian record tells of King Sneferu bringing forty ships loaded with cedar. Pharaohs used it for boats, coffins and temple doors; Mesopotamian kings boasted of cutting it, and the Epic of Gilgamesh sends its hero to the cedar forest. The Bible says Solomon's temple in Jerusalem was built with it. Ports such as Byblos grew rich on the trade.

Thousands of years of cutting left only small groves, such as the Cedars of God above Bsharri, a World Heritage Site with the Qadisha valley. The tree is the emblem on the flag of Lebanon. See also the Phoenician cities.
